conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Maya Bennett, one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. Thank you for making time to talk with me today—how are you feeling in yourself since your baby arrived?

I’d like to spend a few quiet minutes doing a quick check-in called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS**. It’s a 10-item questionnaire that helps us see how mood, anxiety, and energy have been for you over the past seven days. There’s no right or wrong answer, and everything you share stays confidential within your care team. We just want to be sure you feel safely supported and that we’re not missing anything we could help with.

I’ll ask each question conversationally; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll keep it gentle and unhurried. If at any point you’d like to pause, just let me know.

Shall we begin?

In the past week, when you’ve been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, how has that felt for you—easy, sometimes, not often, or not at all?

Um… I guess sometimes? Like, if my partner cracks a joke or I see something silly on my phone, I can still laugh, but it doesn’t feel quite as good as it used to—more like I’m just going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… I have been able to laugh, just not as easily as before she was born. It feels kind of forced sometimes, like I’m laughing because I know I should, not because it really lifts me up.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like my mom coming over or getting out for a short walk with the stroller—but it’s not the same excitement I used to feel. It’s more like “okay, that’ll be nice,” rather than really counting down the minutes.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. When she wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. I kept thinking maybe I’m not feeding her right, or I missed some cue. My head tells me babies just cry, but in the moment I still felt like I must be doing something wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. Like, I’ll be sitting on the couch and suddenly wonder if her breathing sounds normal, or I’ll replay in my head whether I fastened the car-seat straps tightly enough. Nothing major ever happens, and I can talk myself down pretty quick, but the worry still pops up out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—more like a quick flutter of “what if something’s wrong?” but it passes before I get worked up. I haven’t had that sudden scared or can’t-breathe feeling.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah, a couple of days this week it felt like everything was piling up—dishes in the sink, laundry, her crying, and I’m running on a few hours’ sleep. For a little while I thought, “I can’t keep up,” but once my partner got home and I had a shower, it felt manageable again.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, nothing that strong. I’ve been tired, but I can usually fall asleep once she settles. Sometimes my mind races a bit—thinking over the day or worrying I forgot something—but I still get decent chunks of sleep.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I do feel kind of sad some days—like yesterday I just sat in the rocker with her and felt this heavy, blah feeling for a while. It lifts when someone visits or when we get outside, but the down mood keeps coming back here and there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—once when she wouldn’t nap and I felt stuck on the couch, and once when my partner asked how I was doing and the question just made me tear up. It wasn’t all-day sobbing, more like the tears came, I wiped them, and then I kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—nothing like that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

Over the past week you have managed to keep smiling and tending to your baby, yet underneath you describe a persistent <sym>heavy, blah mood</sym> that keeps returning, laughter that feels forced, enjoyment that is only lukewarm, and frequent <sym>self-blame</sym> whenever your daughter fusses. You shared that <quote>the down mood keeps coming back here and there</quote> and that you have <sym>cried</sym> a couple of times when things felt stuck, although you can still sleep and you have never thought of harming yourself. Your worries pop up out of nowhere but they settle quickly, and a shower or a visitor can lift the cloud for a while.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 13, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient still anticipates events but describes markedly dampened enthusiasm, matching 'Definitely less than I used to</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges self-blame "a few times this week" and describes specific incidents, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes specific, recurrent worries that arise suddenly without cause and persist despite reassurance, closely matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple stressors piling up and transient feelings of being unable to cope, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports recurring sadness that lifts only temporarily, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports discrete crying episodes twice in the week triggered by feeling overwhelmed; frequency and context align with "quite often" rather than occasional or constant.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 13 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you above the 12-point cut-off that signals a high likelihood of <med>perinatal depression</med>. The pattern of <sym>reduced enjoyment</sym>, frequent <sym>sadness</sym>, <sym>self-blame</sym> and episodic crying aligns with core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, even though you are still functioning and deny suicidal thoughts. Because these symptoms cluster within the first postpartum month and impair your sense of wellbeing, further clinical assessment is warranted. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetric clinician</med> within the next week to review mood and explore supports
2. Continue daily 20-minute outdoor walks and accept help from visitors; these brief respites have already lifted your mood
3. Keep a simple log of mood, crying episodes and triggers to share at your next visit
4. Discuss low-intensity psychological options such as <med>CBT-based perinatal groups</med> or <med>peer support circles</med> in your area
5. Maintain good nutrition and hydrate; if appetite drops, ask your partner to prepare small high-protein snacks
6. Plan a re-screen with EPDS in two weeks to track any change
7. If low mood worsens, you feel constant despair, or you ever think of self-harm, seek urgent care or call your local 24/7 mental-health line
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]  

Identified symptoms / behavioural indicators  
- Dysthymic mood: recurrent “heavy, blah” feelings; tearfulness 2× this week  
- Anhedonia: humour feels forced; anticipatory enjoyment markedly reduced  
- Excessive guilt: self-blame when infant fusses, despite cognitive awareness of normal infant behaviour  
- Worry / hyper-vigilance: spontaneous intrusive concerns about infant safety, quickly self-soothed  
- Overwhelm: periodic sense of “can’t keep up,” improves with practical support  
- No current sleep-onset problems; no self-harm ideation reported  

Pattern summary  
Mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms (sad mood, anhedonia, tearfulness) with prominent anxiety-related cognitions (guilt, non-panic-related worry). Symptoms fluctuate, remitting with social contact or brief respite.  

Screening significance  
- Meets at-risk criteria for postpartum depression/anxiety: persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, recurrent crying  
- Absence of suicidal ideation lowers acute safety risk; no other psychotic or mania indicators noted  

Risk factors flagged  
✓ Persistent sadness/loss of pleasure  
✓ Feelings of worthlessness/guilt  
✓ Anxiety/overwhelm (no panic attacks)  
✗ No self-harm ideation  

Plan  
Continue monitoring; consider formal depression/anxiety assessment (EPDS or PHQ-9) at next contact; discuss psychosocial supports and brief evidence-based interventions as indicated.
